concepts.name: Green India Mission (GIM): Foundational Framework and Objectives
key_dimensions: GIM as one of the 8 missions under National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) — distinguishing it from other missions
Dual objective: increasing forest/tree cover AND improving quality of existing forests (UPSC trap: it is NOT just about increasing area)
Target of 5 million hectares for afforestation/improvement and additional 5 million hectares for ecosystem services enhancement
GIM's positioning at the intersection of climate adaptation AND mitigation — unlike purely adaptation-focused missions

concepts.name: GIM's Place within NAPCC: Institutional and Thematic Linkages
key_dimensions: Comparison with other NAPCC missions — National Water Mission, Solar Mission, Sustainable Habitat Mission — and areas of overlap with GIM
GIM's specific linkage to National Mission for a Green India vs. National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (both deal with land degradation)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) — distinguishing from other missions nodal ministries
Relationship between GIM and India's Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under Paris Agreement — carbon sink targets

concepts.name: GIM Targets: Quantitative Dimensions and India's NDC Carbon Sink Commitment
key_dimensions: Target to treat 10 million hectares of forest and non-forest lands over 10 years (2015–2025)
India's NDC commitment to create additional carbon sink of 2.5–3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through forest and tree cover by 2030
GIM's contribution toward achieving 33% of geographic area under forest/tree cover — current status vs. target (UPSC factual trap)
Distinction between 'recorded forest area,' 'actual forest cover' (FSI definition), and 'tree cover' — how GIM counts progress differently

concepts.name: Governance Structure of GIM: National, State, and Local Levels
key_dimensions: National Steering Committee chaired by Cabinet Secretary — significance of this high-level oversight
Role of State Forest Departments vs. Gram Sabhas and Joint Forest Management Committees (JFMCs) in implementation
Decentralization trap: GIM mandates community participation but implementation authority rests with states — tension between devolution and control
Convergence mechanism with MGNREGS, CAMPA, and state schemes — GIM is NOT a standalone funding mechanism

concepts.name: Compensatory Afforestation Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA) and GIM Overlap
key_dimensions: CAMPA funds as a key financial source for GIM activities — distinction between CAMPA's legal mandate and GIM's policy mandate
CAMPA Act 2016 vs. GIM objectives: CAMPA is compensatory (reactive), GIM is proactive — UPSC conceptual trap
Net Present Value (NPV) funds under CAMPA vs. Compensatory Afforestation funds — both can support GIM but serve different purposes
Controversy: CAMPA funds historically underutilized; GIM seeks to channelize them — governance accountability issue

concepts.name: Joint Forest Management (JFM) and Community Participation in GIM
key_dimensions: JFM as the primary community-level institution for GIM implementation — role of Van Samrakshan Samitis/JFMCs
Forest Rights Act (FRA) 2006 vs. JFM framework — tension when GIM activities conflict with community forest rights
GIM's requirement of 'informed consent' from gram sabhas before treatment plans — contrast with top-down afforestation drives
Trap: JFM is a state government circular-based system, NOT a statutory body — implications for legal enforceability under GIM

concepts.name: Types of Land Targeted Under GIM: Forest vs. Non-Forest Interventions
key_dimensions: Five landscape types under GIM: moderately dense forests, degraded forests, grasslands/wetlands, agroforestry lands, and urban/peri-urban areas
Distinction: GIM covers BOTH forest land (under MoEFCC jurisdiction) AND non-forest degraded land (under multiple ministry jurisdictions) — coordination challenge
Agroforestry promotion under GIM — linkage with National Agroforestry Policy 2014
Urban greening component: GIM's overlap with Smart Cities Mission and AMRUT for urban tree cover — institutional duplication trap

concepts.name: Forest Survey of India (FSI) Biennial Assessment and GIM Progress Measurement
key_dimensions: FSI's India State of Forest Report (ISFR) as primary monitoring tool for GIM targets — published every 2 years
Methodological trap: FSI uses satellite-based classification — orchards, plantations, and bamboo groves counted as 'tree cover' but not always as 'forest cover'
Open Forest, Moderately Dense Forest, Very Dense Forest — FSI categories and how GIM measures quality improvement, not just quantity
UPSC trap: increase in recorded forest cover in ISFR does NOT necessarily mean GIM success — distinction between natural regeneration and planted cover

concepts.name: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services Focus in GIM
key_dimensions: GIM explicitly includes biodiversity conservation as a co-benefit, linking it to Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) commitments
Ecosystem services framework: GIM covers provisioning, regulating, cultural, and supporting services — not just timber/carbon
Linkage with National Biodiversity Action Plan (NBAP) and Aichi Biodiversity Targets (now Kunming-Montreal GBF targets)
Trap: GIM is sometimes conflated with a pure 'plantation drive' — but its mandate explicitly rejects monoculture plantations in favor of native species diversity

concepts.name: GIM and Climate Change: Mitigation vs. Adaptation Dual Role
key_dimensions: GIM as a mitigation tool: forests as carbon sinks contributing to NDC targets under Paris Agreement
GIM as an adaptation tool: improving watershed functions, reducing landslides, moderating local climate — adaptation benefits often understated in UPSC answers
REDD+ mechanism (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation) — how GIM aligns with international REDD+ framework for carbon credits
Trap: GIM is listed under NAPCC as a mitigation AND adaptation mission — candidates often classify it as only one

concepts.name: Funding Mechanism of GIM: Central Assistance, State Share, and Convergence
key_dimensions: GIM funding pattern: 90:10 (Centre:State) for NE and Himalayan states; 75:25 for other states — similar to other Centrally Sponsored Schemes
Convergence with MGNREGS for labor costs in afforestation — GIM provides material costs while MGNREGS provides wage component
International climate finance: GIM explicitly seeks Green Climate Fund (GCF) and bilateral climate finance — linkage with India's climate diplomacy
UPSC trap: GIM does NOT have a dedicated independent fund — it operates through existing government financial channels and CAMPA convergence

concepts.name: GIM and Forest Rights Act (FRA) 2006: Convergence and Conflict
key_dimensions: FRA recognizes community forest resource (CFR) rights — GIM activities on CFR areas require gram sabha approval, creating potential delays
Positive convergence: GIM can empower CFR right-holders to manage and improve forests, aligning with community-based conservation
Conflict scenario: GIM afforestation on 'degraded land' that is actually under community use/encroachment — displacement risk
Trap: FRA and GIM are under the SAME nodal ministry (MoEFCC) but operate under different legal/policy frameworks — implementation contradictions are real

concepts.name: Agroforestry Promotion Under GIM and Its Socioeconomic Dimensions
key_dimensions: GIM targets 2 million hectares of agroforestry on private/community lands — distinguishing this from government forest land targets
National Agroforestry Policy 2014 as the complementary policy — GIM provides the financial mechanism for its implementation
Income generation for farmers through timber, NTFPs (Non-Timber Forest Products), and carbon credits — poverty-environment nexus
UPSC trap: Agroforestry under GIM is counted toward India's 'tree cover' target in NDC, but trees on agricultural land are NOT classified as 'forests' under Indian Forest Act 1927

concepts.name: Non-Timber Forest Products (NTFPs) and Livelihood Linkages in GIM
key_dimensions: GIM explicitly links forest improvement with livelihood enhancement through NTFPs — bamboo, medicinal plants, honey, etc.
Bamboo: reclassified as 'grass' (not tree) under Indian Forest Act Amendment 2017 — significance for GIM's bamboo-based livelihood component
Van Dhan Vikas Kendras (under TRIFED) as complementary institutions for NTFP value addition — GIM-TRIFED convergence
Trap: GIM's livelihood component is often confused with purely economic forestry — GIM mandates sustainable harvesting, not commercial exploitation

concepts.name: GIM Implementation Challenges: Governance, Land Tenure, and Inter-Ministry Coordination
key_dimensions: Land ownership trap: GIM targets include revenue wastelands (under state Revenue Dept.), forest lands (MoEFCC), and private lands — different legal regimes for each
Inter-ministry coordination failure: degraded lands under Ministry of Rural Development, Agriculture, and Tribal Affairs also fall under GIM scope
CAG audit findings on GIM: delays in preparation of micro-plans, poor community mobilization, and inadequate monitoring — governance accountability angle
Invasive alien species (Lantana camara, Prosopis juliflora) on degraded lands — GIM's treatment plans must address invasives, but this is rarely implemented systematically

concepts.name: GIM's Relationship with State-Level Forest Policies and Compensatory Afforestation
key_dimensions: States must align their State Action Plans on Climate Change (SAPCCs) with GIM targets — federal coordination mechanism
Compensatory afforestation under Forest Conservation Act 1980: diversion of forest land requires equivalent afforestation — GIM seeks to improve quality of such compensatory plantations
Trap: Compensatory afforestation (legal requirement) is different from GIM afforestation (policy-driven) — both count toward forest cover but have different governance mechanisms
States with highest forest cover (Madhya Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh) vs. states with most forest degradation — GIM prioritization logic

concepts.name: Urban Forestry and Peri-Urban Greening Under GIM
key_dimensions: GIM includes urban/peri-urban component — one of the five landscape types specifically targeting city green cover
Overlap with Smart Cities Mission, AMRUT, and National Urban Policy — risk of institutional duplication and double-counting of tree cover
Urban heat island mitigation through GIM's urban greening — climate adaptation co-benefit often overlooked

Trap: Urban trees are counted as 'tree cover' by FSI but NOT as 'forest cover' — GIM's urban component contributes to NDC tree cover target but NOT to the 33% forest cover target under National Forest Policy 1988

concepts.name: National Forest Policy 1988 and GIM: Alignment and Gaps
key_dimensions: National Forest Policy 1988 mandates 33% of geographic area under forest/tree cover — GIM is the primary implementation vehicle for this target
Policy 1988 emphasis on 'social forestry' and community involvement — GIM operationalizes this through JFM and CFR frameworks
Gap: National Forest Policy 1988 is not a legislation but a policy — no legal enforceability, making GIM targets aspirational rather than mandatory
New Draft National Forest Policy 2018 (not yet finalized) — proposed changes that would affect GIM's implementation mandate, including private sector participation

concepts.name: REDD+ and International Climate Finance Linkages with GIM
key_dimensions: REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation) under UNFCCC — GIM's afforestation and degradation reduction activities are REDD+-eligible
India's REDD+ National Strategy: how GIM activities generate internationally recognized emission reductions/removals
Trap: REDD+ provides results-based payments (payment after verified outcomes), while GIM is an input-based government scheme — India is pursuing BOTH simultaneously
Green Climate Fund (GCF) and bilateral climate finance (Germany's GIZ, JICA Japan) supporting GIM — India's use of international climate finance for domestic forest governance

concepts.name: Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) Framework Under GIM
key_dimensions: GIM's MRV system: combination of FSI satellite assessments, ground-truthing by state forest departments, and social audits by gram sabhas
Carbon stock assessment methodology: GIM uses IPCC-approved tier-based methodology for reporting forest carbon — linkage with India's Biennial Update Reports (BURs) to UNFCCC
Trap: GIM's success is measured by area treated (input indicator), NOT by carbon sequestered or biodiversity improved (outcome indicators) — a major monitoring design flaw
Role of ISRO's National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) in providing satellite data for GIM monitoring — science-policy interface
